questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the most common charting mistake?
options: Picking a chart type that can't actually answer the real question behind the data, regardless of how good it looks
Always using bar charts for everything
Making charts too small to read
questions.explain: A well-formatted chart still fails if it's the wrong type for the question — like a pie chart used to show a trend over time, which a pie chart has no way to represent at all.

questions.q: Where does Excel's Recommended Charts feature live?
options: Data tab > Get & Transform Data group
questions.explain: Select your data and use Insert > Recommended Charts (in the Charts group) to see Excel's suggested chart types for that data's shape.

questions.q: Why is Excel's Recommended Charts suggestion described as 'a starting point, not a verdict'?
options: Because it reasons from your data's shape, not from the actual business question you're trying to answer with the chart
Because it is frequently broken and produces errors
Because it only works in Excel for the web, not desktop
Because it requires a paid Microsoft 365 subscription to use
questions.explain: Recommended Charts scans column/category structure, but has no idea what real-world question you're asking — so its suggestion should always be checked against your actual question, not accepted automatically.

questions.q: Which chart type is built specifically to show a value changing over a continuous period, and should never be replaced with a pie chart?
questions.explain: Line charts show change over a continuous axis like time. A pie chart has no concept of order or time at all, making it the wrong tool for a trend question.

questions.q: You want to know whether one numeric variable tends to move together with another — for example, whether higher marketing spend correlates with higher sales. Which chart family fits this question?
options: Stacked column chart (composition of a whole)
questions.explain: A scatter chart plots two numeric measures against each other, making a correlation (or its absence) visible — a job bar and line charts aren't built to do.
